project.name: Not Arbitrary 14 — The Moon in 'Liver' Is Meat

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Look at the Chinese words for liver, lung, elbow and belly. Every one of them has the character for the moon down its left side.
entries.direction: Warm, unhurried, a little conspiratorial. Let the four body parts breathe as a list, then land 'the moon' with a small smile.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: None of them has anything to do with the moon. That shape is three different pictures, squeezed over two thousand years into the same four strokes.
entries.direction: Plain and clear. A small pause after 'the moon', then a little lift on 'three different pictures'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The first really is the moon. The oldest Chinese writing, cut into bone more than three thousand years ago, draws it as a crescent.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: As the script grew square, the curve became a frame, with two short bars inside it.
entries.direction: Unhurried, as if watching it happen.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The second is a piece of meat. Its oldest drawings show a slice, with lines across it. Squeezed into the side of a character, it stood up straight and lost its curves, until it matched the moon.
entries.direction: Dry and a little amused on 'a piece of meat'. Then matter of fact, building slightly to 'until it matched the moon'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: That is why so much of the body is written with it. A liver, a lung, an elbow and a belly are all meat.
entries.direction: Warm. Land 'are all meat' simply, with no lift.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The third is a boat: a long hull, with bars across it.
entries.direction: The turn of the film. Slow down, and a definite pause after 'The third is a boat'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The character for 'in front' began as a foot, standing in a boat that is moving forward.
entries.direction: Light and pleased with the picture. Say 'in front' as an ordinary English phrase.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: More than two thousand years ago, clerks simplifying the script to write it faster shrank the foot to two ticks and a line, and the boat to the moon's four strokes.
entries.direction: Plain, steady narration. A small beat before 'and the boat to the moon's four strokes'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: And when the first emperor of China took a word for 'I' that only an emperor could use, it was written with a boat as well.
entries.direction: A little wry. The word 'I' is the pronoun, said clearly in the middle of the sentence.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Careful printers still told the three apart. China's great dictionary of seventeen sixteen prints three versions: the moon's bars stop short, the meat's bars reach across, and the boat has two dots.
entries.direction: A new thread, so lift slightly. Give the three versions the same shape, one after another.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: In the twentieth century, China and Japan made all three identical, and the shape they chose was the meat's. Taiwan and Hong Kong still print the meat apart.
entries.direction: Matter of fact, with a small dry smile on 'the shape they chose was the meat's'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: And in Japan and in Korea, the meat has kept a name of its own. In both languages, it means the meat moon.
entries.direction: Warm, a small smile on 'the meat moon'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Three pictures: the moon in the sky, a slice of meat, and a boat going forward, squeezed into one shape.
entries.direction: Gather it up. Warm, not a summary read.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: So the moon in the word for liver was never the moon. Today, the moon itself is printed like meat.
entries.direction: Land it and stop, no lift at the end - but say the final words, 'printed like meat', fully and clearly.
